A1.justification: Both PDFs describe DEFT and retain matching core definitions and algorithms. Their text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison without material extraction gaps.

before.justification: v1 reports original latency and IO measurements for sorting and document-merging workloads, including averages over 100 trees in Table 4 and per-iteration results in Figure 8.

after.justification: v2 reports original latency and IO measurements across few-shot prompting, four reasoning tasks, and speculative decoding, plus ablations and bottleneck analyses in Section 4 and Appendix A.6.

M1.justification: The core attention algorithms persist: Algorithms 1–4 match across versions after the DEFT-Subtree-to-DEFT-Flatten rename. v2 reports adapting DEFT kernels to paged as well as unpaged KV storage (Table 5 and Appendix A.1), a limited system extension. Balanced splitting, bit masks, and global reduction already appear in v1.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates sorting 128 numbers and document merging. v2 retains these and adds keyword counting, set intersection, and APPS-based few-shot prompting and speculative-decoding workloads (Tables 6–7 and 10), substantially broadening the tasks and tree-structured inference scenarios evaluated.

E2.justification: Radix Attention from SGLang becomes an evaluated comparator, including on the retained reasoning tasks, alongside Flash-Decoding and Tree Attention-Medusa (v2 Tables 7, 11–12). It provides the strongest end-to-end baseline. The stated Flash-Decoding implementation also changes from CUDA in v1 Section 4.1 to Triton in v2 Table 5.

E3.justification: Section 4.1 changes the stated model from Llama2-7B-HF to Llama3-8B, although v2's citation still identifies Llama 2. v2 introduces explicit paged/unpaged configurations, separate attention timing, and expanded partial-result IO accounting. New protocols include approximately 4,000-token prompts with 400 decoding iterations and speculative token trees of 32–256 queries.

E4.justification: v2 adds a Node-versus-Flatten split ablation linked to node-length dispersion (Figure 5), memory-management latency decompositions (Figures 4 and 13), and tree-width sensitivity analysis (Figure 14). v1's thought-length distributions and task-averaged reasoning iteration plots (Figures 7–8) are not retained. The questions investigated therefore change substantially.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-seed timing experiments, confidence intervals, significance tests, or defined uncertainty estimates for performance. v2 Figure 5's standard deviation describes tree-node lengths, not uncertainty in measured speedups; v1's 100 trees are workload samples rather than reported repeated runs.

E6.justification: Reasoning measurements are replaced under revised model and memory settings: DEFT-Node sorting/document latency is 305/272 seconds in v1 Table 4 versus 114.06/81.87 seconds in v2 Table 11. v2 adds extensive Flatten, Radix, and new-task results, including 1.03–1.10× reasoning and up to 2.52× speculative end-to-end speedups over Radix. These do not establish same-setting gains over v1.

T1.justification: The core definitions and prefix-sharing argument remain. v2 Table 4 introduces a QKV-group factor into query IO accounting and includes scaling, mask, and masked-logit costs; the worked crossover changes from 32 to 29 queries. Appendix A.3 also supplies an explicit LogSumExp attention-merging argument in Equation 2.

C1.justification: The headline contribution broadens from tree-search reasoning to general tree-structured inference, explicitly encompassing few-shot prompting and speculative decoding. v2 promotes both Node and Flatten implementations and replaces the two-task 1.7–2.4× claim with separate end-to-end and attention claims of up to 2.52× and 3.82× across three workload families.

C2.justification: v2 explains how KV materialization dominates unpaged execution and how paging shifts the bottleneck toward attention (Section 4.2). It attributes modest reasoning gains to narrow trees and limited attention overhead, and explicitly limits substantial gains to sufficiently large shared contexts or numerous queries (Sections 4.3 and 5). Appendix A.6 additionally explains declining benefits as suffixes grow.

D1.justification: v2 supplements the retained pseudocode with a backend/paging matrix, an explicit depth-first layout description, and workload specifications covering stopping criteria, tree shapes, and recorded speculative acceptance lengths (Tables 5–6 and 10; Appendix A.5). However, v1's explicit 100-tree workload count is no longer reported.

R1.justification: Section 2 and new Appendix A.3 substantially expand positioning against ChunkAttention, Hydragen, and Bifurcated Attention. Table 8 distinguishes shared IO-reduction ideas from DEFT's claimed support for deeper trees and balanced workloads. Additional citations cover Prompt Cache, APPS, few-shot learning, self-consistency, and inference systems.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, and contribution narrative are substantially rewritten around general tree-structured inference. System, kernel, and workload explanations are reorganized between the main text and appendices; experiments gain dedicated bottleneck and ablation sections, and the appendix gains a contents list and expanded organization.

P2.justification: The interaction and QKV-grouping diagrams are substantially redrawn, and results are reorganized into separate attention, end-to-end, and IO tables. New bottleneck, split-ablation, and width-sensitivity plots accompany these changes. Existing diagrams are also relocated, including v1 Figures 2 and 5 becoming v2 Figures 6 and 11, while the document template changes.

improvement.justification: v1 tests only Node on two reasoning workloads and leaves its balanced variant without results. v2 evaluates that variant, introduces the stronger paged Radix comparator, and separates attention gains from memory-management costs through breakdowns and ablations. Broader workloads and explicit limits substantially strengthen the evidence and interpretation of speedups. Reporting remains imperfect: v2 omits the earlier 100-tree count and has a model-label/citation mismatch. These weaknesses do not outweigh the substantial empirical and analytical gains.
